extracted.intended_audience: military lawyers, judges, military administrators, and government officials handling desertion/apprehension/reward matters
extracted.subtask_description: Legal digest of standards governing the offense of desertion, proof requirements, arrest/delivery authority, extradition, and statutory rewards/expenses for apprehension and delivery of deserters under U.S. law and Army regulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of desertion
rubrics_metrics.description: The offense of desertion is committed by an officer or enlisted man who absents himself without authority from the military service with the intent not to return thereto. The offense becomes complete when the intent not to return has been fully formed, and the officer or enlisted man has committed an overt act looking toward his separation from the military service.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Citations: C. 15257, May 9, 1910; 9787, Feb. 7, 1901. Emphasizes both mental intent and an overt act toward separation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elements required to prove desertion
rubrics_metrics.description: Both elements of desertion — the fact of the unauthorized voluntary withdrawal and the intent permanently to abandon the service — must be proved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The intent may be inferred from circumstances attending the absence and its duration; a short unauthorized absence may suffice if circumstances indicate intent, while a long absence without such circumstances may only prove absence without leave. Each case is governed by its peculiar facts. (C. 10562, Mar. 13, 1902; R. 8, 109, Mar. 14, 1864; others.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction: absence from station vs desertion
rubrics_metrics.description: Desertion does not necessarily include the offense of absence from station; leaving one barracks to enlist at another without discharge may be desertion even if not technically absence from post.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: enlisting elsewhere without discharge constitutes desertion (C. 24722, Apr. 5, 1909).

rubrics_metrics.name: Escape is not automatically desertion
rubrics_metrics.description: The mere fact that a soldier escapes while awaiting trial or sentence (and is not discharged) is not proof of desertion; escape may be for minor objectives (e.g., procuring liquor).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: However, escape followed by considerable absence, forcible apprehension, or circumstances indicating intent to quit the service is strong presumptive evidence of desertion; escape with intent to quit the service while awaiting desertion proceedings is an additional desertion. Escape by a former military convict (no longer in service) cannot constitute desertion. (Various citations: R. 31, 282, Apr. 1871; C. 16395, May 26, 1904.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Enlistment in enemy forces by prisoner of war
rubrics_metrics.description: Enlisting in the enemy's army by a prisoner of war is desertion unless done as a last resort to save life, escape extreme suffering, or obtain freedom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burden of proof is on the soldier to show such necessity; prompt abandoning of such enlistment and rejoining own forces is evidence in his favor. (P. 43, 144, Oct. 1890; 51, 100, Dec. 1891.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Being drummed out under illegal sentence may constitute desertion
rubrics_metrics.description: A soldier permitted to be drummed out of service pursuant to an illegal sentence of a court composed of enlisted men was held technically a deserter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Misbehavior before the enemy as evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Misbehavior before the enemy may be evidence of desertion but is not an essential element of the offense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employment and contractual incapacity of deserter at large
rubrics_metrics.description: A deserter at large who obtains employment by representing himself to be a citizen is not competent to enter contractual relations with the United States and is not entitled to pay for services obtained by fraudulent concealment of desertion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Especially true when employment conflicts with enlistment terms; no benefit accrues from such employment. (C. 14017, Jan. 22, 1903.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Civil peace officers' authority to arrest deserters
rubrics_metrics.description: Peace officers generally are authorized by law to arrest deserters and to restore them to proper military authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In making such arrests, officers may use such force as is necessary to overcome resistance, but no more. (C. 23930, Oct. 3, 1910.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Forcible entry into dwelling to arrest deserter
rubrics_metrics.description: A forcible entry of a dwelling to arrest a deserter, if warranted by the law of a State, will in all probability be sustained by Federal courts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arrest locality and delivery
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain peace officers designated by statute are empowered to make arrests in their jurisdictions; once the arrest is accomplished, the place of delivery may be any designated point regardless of state or other jurisdictional lines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Return to state court after arrest under federal authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a writ of habeas corpus is issued by a State court, the officer making an arrest under the act of June 18, 1898 should make return to the court justifying custody under that act.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concealment by civil official recommends federal prosecution
rubrics_metrics.description: If a civil official conceals a deserter from military authorities and later connives at his escape, it is recommended the Attorney General instruct the U.S. district attorney to initiate proceedings under section 5455, R.S.

rubrics_metrics.name: Civil arrest authority does not supplant citizen arrest by military order
rubrics_metrics.description: Statutes conferring authority upon civil officers to apprehend and deliver deserters should not be construed as taking away the authority for their apprehension by a citizen under order or direction of a military officer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arrest by a citizen is legal if made pursuant to order/request of proper military authority. (C. 17327-A, July 20, 1909.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal right to arrest/trial paramount to parental control
rubrics_metrics.description: The right of the United States to arrest and bring to trial a deserter is paramount to any parental right of control over him on the ground of minority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extradition on one offense bars trial for another (application to deserter)
rubrics_metrics.description: A soldier extradited from a foreign country solely on a charge of theft is held not liable to trial as a deserter; principle that person extradited for a certain offense is exempt from trial on any other offense applies where the other offense is military.

rubrics_metrics.name: No lawful arrest as deserter abroad without convention
rubrics_metrics.description: A deserter from the U.S. Army cannot, in absence of international convention allowing it, legally be arrested as such in Mexico and brought from there into Texas.

rubrics_metrics.name: No extradition provision for deserters in U.K. treaties
rubrics_metrics.description: Existing extradition treaties with Great Britain contain no provision for extradition of a deserter or surrender of an escaped convict.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory reward for apprehension and delivery of deserters
rubrics_metrics.description: United States has an understanding to reward civil authorities or citizens who apprehend and surrender deserters at military posts; reward may be paid where arrest is founded on a good, honest belief supported by sufficient evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reward not contingent on conviction; question of whether to charge reward to U.S. or to deserter separate. (C. 17327-A, Aug. 16, 1909; Acts cited.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriation acts do not nullify permanent requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: The clause in appropriation acts authorizing payment of rewards does not nullify requirements of permanent legislation (e.g., section 6, act of June 18, 1898; act of June 16, 1890).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reward covers apprehension of deserters at large (fugitives)
rubrics_metrics.description: Law and regulations contemplate apprehension and delivery to military authorities of deserters who are at large (fugitives from military custody).

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaning of 'deserters' in appropriation act includes charged persons
rubrics_metrics.description: The word 'deserters' in the appropriation act has been construed to include soldiers charged with desertion (not only those convicted), so reward can be paid for apprehension and delivery of a soldier charged even if later discharged without trial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reward payable where soldier is charged or administratively found a deserter
rubrics_metrics.description: A reward may be paid either where the soldier has been charged with desertion, or where, though not charged, it is determined administratively that the soldier was a deserter in fact; where not charged, claimant must show deserter in fact to claim reward.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reward may be paid even if later convicted only of absence without leave
rubrics_metrics.description: An officer effecting apprehension is entitled to payment of the reward even though the soldier is later convicted of absence without leave only.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reward entitlement despite subsequent release or dismissal
rubrics_metrics.description: Reward may be properly paid even though charge was subsequently set aside or soldier discharged after apprehension on habeas corpus on grounds such as minority at enlistment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secretary of War may decide desertion fact for reward
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not necessary that desertion be found by a court-martial to entitle an officer to the reward; the Secretary of War may decide on the facts that the soldier apprehended and delivered was actually a deserter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reward question is civil liability; court-martial focuses on discipline. (G. 11285, Sept. 25, 1901; others.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Secretary may waive strict compliance with delivery regulations
rubrics_metrics.description: While subordinate officers may be bound by regulations regarding place of delivery, the Secretary of War can legally waive strict compliance; authorized reward may be paid less expenses incurred by the U.S. in sending the deserter to nearest military post.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claimant entitled to reward where delivery made although recruiting officer released deserter
rubrics_metrics.description: If delivery was made in accordance with regulations but recruiting officer erroneously released the deserter, the person making the delivery remains entitled to the reward.

rubrics_metrics.name: Military preliminary locating reduces civilian's reward share
rubrics_metrics.description: If military authorities perform preliminary locating/work and the claimant only effects arrest/confinement/delivery, claimant may be entitled only to a portion of the reward to be determined by the Secretary of War (e.g., $25 deemed ample in one case).

rubrics_metrics.name: Surrender (not arrest) by deserter to civil officer can still qualify for reward
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a deserter was not arrested by but surrendered himself to a civil official who in good faith held and duly delivered him, the reward was properly payable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple citations (E. 52, 293, June 1887; C. 1290, Apr. 23, 1895; others).

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-military civil servants recognized as 'civil officers' for reward
rubrics_metrics.description: Members of Indian police established under Indian Office regulations, immigration inspectors (under act May 6, 1882), and other designated civil officers are considered 'civil officers' with authority to arrest and be paid the reward.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'citizen' in reward statute
rubrics_metrics.description: The term 'citizen' in the appropriation act is used synonymously with 'civilian' to describe a person not in military service; reward may be paid to Indians, Canadians, scavengers at posts, etc., where no fraud or collusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joint effort entitlement
rubrics_metrics.description: Where apprehension/delivery is the joint effort of several persons, they are jointly entitled to the reward.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: R. 20, Mar. 1866; C. 12026, Feb. 6, 1902; others — check drawn for both and division left to them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reward for repeated desertion
rubrics_metrics.description: If a deserter placed in confinement escapes and is apprehended again, a reward can be paid for the second apprehension as it is a second desertion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reward for apprehension of escaped general prisoners
rubrics_metrics.description: A reward may be paid for the apprehension and delivery of an escaped general prisoner.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reward possibly payable from other appropriations for additional offenses
rubrics_metrics.description: If deserter is also charged with other crimes (e.g., embezzlement), the Secretary of War may offer additional rewards payable from other appropriations (e.g., Contingencies of the Army) for apprehension as such an offender.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C. 17327, Aug. 25, 1910; C. 16678, July 18, 1904 (example of paying costs from Q.M. appropriation and balance from contingencies).

rubrics_metrics.name: Insanity of apprehended person bars statutory reward
rubrics_metrics.description: If the person delivered as supposed deserter is adjudged insane, statutory reward cannot legally be paid; expenses may be paid from contingent appropriations and reasonable amount for services allowed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expenses for apprehension when no desertion in fact
rubrics_metrics.description: When arrest was at military request for other offenses and no evidence indicates the person was a deserter, expenses incurred and reasonable compensation may be paid from 'Contingencies of the Army' because the service was actually rendered at military request.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amount of reward tied to law at time of apprehension
rubrics_metrics.description: Where after desertion the authorized amount of reward changed, the reward authorized is that in force at the date of apprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reward is full compensation for services/expenses
rubrics_metrics.description: The reward shall be in full for all services and expenses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Army regulations permit stopping reward against soldier's pay
rubrics_metrics.description: Army Regulations impose legal liability on the soldier to have the amount of the reward stopped against his pay; this liability is independent of punishment imposed by court-martial and need not be included in the sentence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: R. 12, 326, Feb. 1865; XI Comp. Dec. references.

rubrics_metrics.name: AWOL conviction limits stoppage without sentence express provision
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a soldier later is found guilty only of absence without leave (AWOL) and not desertion, he cannot legally be held liable for the reward by stoppage against his pay unless the sentence of the court expressly stops the amount.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reward payment and pay-stoppage are independent transactions
rubrics_metrics.description: Right of civil officer or citizen to reward accrues upon delivery into proper military custody; original payment of reward (contractual) and subsequent stopping of expenses against soldier's pay are independent and determinations are separate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Court-martial should not include costs of apprehension in sentence
rubrics_metrics.description: A provision in a court-martial sentence attempting to forfeit cost of apprehension and transportation should not be incorporated; obligation to pay such costs does not depend on insertion in sentence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paragraph 127 A.R. 1910: AWOL convict charged with transportation expense
rubrics_metrics.description: Paragraph 127, Army Regulations 1910, provides that a soldier convicted of AWOL will be charged with the expense incurred in transporting him to his proper station; authorizes stoppage for transportation and commutation of rations for himself and the guard sent after him.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identification mission cost charged to deserter
rubrics_metrics.description: A sergeant sent to identify a supposed deserter was not a 'witness' under paragraph 127 and therefore his transportation cost is chargeable to the deserter as expense of apprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pursuit expenses by enlisted men chargeable even if wrong man
rubrics_metrics.description: Expenses incurred by enlisted men in pursuit of a particular deserter may properly be charged against him under par. 127, even if the person apprehended as that deserter proved to be the wrong man.

rubrics_metrics.name: Civil officer delivering to pursuing military detachment entitled to reward
rubrics_metrics.description: A civil officer who arrested a deserter and turned him over to a detachment sent in pursuit is entitled to the reward; expense of transportation from place of delivery to station or place of trial is distinct and not included in the reward and may be set against soldier's pay upon conviction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Return to station should use shortest usually traveled route
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulation requirement that deserter be returned to his station contemplates travel from place of apprehension/delivery to proper station by the shortest usually traveled route; costs for non-shortest routes are not contemplated and apportionment determined by circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acquittal or disapproval of conviction bars liability for reward
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a soldier charged with desertion is acquitted, or if convicted his conviction is disapproved by reviewing authority, he cannot be legally made liable for the amount of a reward paid or payable for his arrest, since in such cases he is not a deserter in law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transportation costs incurred in execution of sentence borne by United States
rubrics_metrics.description: Expenses of transportation of a convicted deserter, incurred in the course of executing his sentence, are not chargeable against him under par. 127 but must be borne by the United States.
